Write the introduction to a guide for a REST API that manages calendar bookings. Around 200 words.

# Introduction

The Bookings API gives your application programmatic control over a shared calendar: creating appointments, moving them, cancelling them, and querying what time remains open. If you have ever written a scheduling feature by hand, you know the hard part is not storing a start time and an end time. It is answering "can this go here?" correctly when three people are booking the same 2 p.m. slot from three time zones.

This guide covers the whole surface. You will find the resource model first (calendars, availability windows, bookings, and attendees), then authentication, then a walkthrough that takes you from an empty calendar to a confirmed booking with reminders attached. Later sections deal with the situations that break naive implementations: recurring events, daylight-saving transitions, double-booking conflicts, and webhook delivery when a client cancels while your server is offline.

Every endpoint speaks JSON over HTTPS. Requests carry a bearer token; responses carry an ETag you can use for conditional updates. Times are ISO 8601 with an explicit offset, and any endpoint that accepts a time range also accepts an IANA time zone name so you never have to do the arithmetic yourself.

Start with Quickstart if you want a working request in five minutes. Start with Resource Model if you are designing a schema around this API.

## Authentication

Every request needs a bearer token in the `Authorization` header. Tokens come in two kinds. A user token, obtained through the OAuth flow, acts on behalf of one person and can only touch calendars that person can see. A service token, issued from the dashboard, acts on behalf of your application and can read and write any calendar in your workspace, which makes it the right choice for backend jobs and the wrong choice for anything running in a browser. Both kinds carry scopes, and the API rejects a request whose token lacks the scope for that endpoint with a 403 naming the scope it wanted. User tokens expire after one hour; refresh them with the refresh token you received alongside, and expect a new refresh token in the response, since the old one stops working the moment you use it. Service tokens do not expire, so rotate them yourself and keep two active during a rotation to avoid a gap. All requests go over HTTPS on port 443, and a request that arrives over plain HTTP gets a 400 rather than a redirect, so a leaked token cannot travel in cleartext by accident. Rate limits apply per token, not per calendar: 600 requests a minute for service tokens, 120 for user tokens, reported in the `X-RateLimit-Remaining` header on every response.

## Authentication

Before the API will do anything for you, it needs to know who you are. You prove that by sending a token: a long string of random characters that works like a password your program can carry around. Every request you make includes a header (an extra line of information attached to the request) that reads `Authorization: Bearer` followed by your token. Leave it off and you get back an error saying 401, which is the code for "I don't know who you are."

There are two kinds of token. A user token stands in for one person, and it can only reach the calendars that person could open by hand. Your app gets one by sending the person through a login screen, where they approve your access. A service token stands in for your app itself and can reach every calendar in your workspace. Create one from the dashboard and keep it on your own server, never in a web page or mobile app, since anyone who reads it gets the same access you have.

User tokens stop working after an hour. When that happens, you trade a second string called a refresh token for a fresh pair, and the old refresh token dies at that moment, so save the new one. Service tokens last until you replace them.

Two more rules. Always call the API at an address beginning `https://`, since plain `http://` requests are refused outright rather than quietly forwarded. And there is a cap on how often you can call: 120 requests a minute on a user token, 600 on a service token. Each response tells you how many you have left in a header named `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, so you can slow down before you hit the wall.
